common_name: Violet Queen Echeveria (Pink-Blushed Elegans Hybrid Hens and Chicks)

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright light to full sun in fast-draining, gritty cactus-and-succulent mix; Violet Queen, a hybrid of Echeveria elegans bred by Santa Barbara horticulturalist E.O. Orpet, forms open rosettes of long, narrow, silver-green leaves that curve gently toward the tips.

directions: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright light to full sun in fast-draining, gritty cactus-and-succulent mix. Violet Queen forms an open, lotus-blossom-shaped rosette up to 6 inches across of long, narrow, silver-green leaves coated in a waxy farina, with tips and margins that blush rose-pink to violet under bright light, cool nights, and light frost, most vividly in late fall and winter. It offsets freely, quickly forming a dense mounding cluster that can be divided to start new plants. Nodding, pinkish-orange, bell-shaped flowers appear on slender, unbranched stalks in spring. Water only when the soil is fully dry, and provide bright light to keep the rosette compact and richly colored rather than stretched and green.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright light to full sun in fast-draining, gritty cactus-and-succulent mix; Lipstick forms a crisp, agave-like rosette of fleshy, sharp-pointed, bright green leaves edged in vivid crimson-red, with the red intensifying under stronger sun.

directions: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright light to full sun in fast-draining, gritty cactus-and-succulent mix. Lipstick forms a tight, symmetrical rosette of ovate-deltoid, spine-tipped, bright green leaves up to 3 inches long that closely resemble a small agave, each rimmed in a vivid crimson-red margin that becomes more conspicuous with stronger sunlight. It offsets very freely, with pups hugging close to the mother rosette to form a tidy cluster over time. In spring and early summer it sends up flowering spikes of red blooms with yellow tips. Water only when the soil is fully dry, avoid wetting the leaves, and provide bright light for the boldest red edge coloration.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

common_name: Cinderella Echeveria (Yellow-Green Rosette with Red Margins)

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright light to full sun in fast-draining, gritty cactus-and-succulent mix; Cinderella, an uncommon collector's cultivar, forms a moderately tight rosette of longer yellowish-green leaves that turn greener toward the center, edged in deep pointed red that deepens with more sun.

directions: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright light to full sun in fast-draining, gritty cactus-and-succulent mix. Cinderella forms a moderately tight rosette of elongated, yellowish-green leaves that shift greener toward the center, with pointed margins that flush a deep red under bright light and cool temperatures. An uncommon, sought-after collector's cultivar, it branches and develops a visible stem as it matures, raising the rosette like a small candelabra. Water only when the soil is fully dry, avoid wetting the leaves, and provide bright light to bring out the strongest red-margin contrast.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

common_name: Harbour Lights Jade Plant (Winter Red-Flushed Jade)

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright light to full sun in fast-draining, gritty cactus-and-succulent mix; Harbour Lights is a compact jade cultivar whose small green leaves flush an intense sunset red through the cool winter months.

directions: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright light to full sun in fast-draining, gritty cactus-and-succulent mix. Harbour Lights forms a dense, bonsai-like shrub on a stubby trunk, with relatively small, fleshy leaves that stay green through the warmer months and turn an intense sunset red as cool weather arrives in fall and winter, among the most dramatic seasonal color-changers of the jade plant cultivars. Small clusters of pinkish-white, star-shaped flowers appear at the branch tips from late autumn into early winter. It tolerates sandy, coastal conditions better than many succulents. Water only when the soil is fully dry, and provide bright light and cool nights for the deepest winter red.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

common_name: Variegated Cathedral Window Haworthia (Cream-Striped Window Haworthia)

planting.note: Separate rosette offsets from established clumps in spring and pot in well-drained, gritty succulent mix; this variegated form of cathedral window haworthia forms stemless rosettes of thick, boat-shaped leaves striped in light green and cream, and needs a bit more light than the solid-green species since the pale tissue lacks chlorophyll.

directions: Grow in bright indirect light, with a bit more sun exposure than the solid-green species, in a shallow pot of gritty, fast-draining cactus mix, letting the soil dry out between waterings. This variegated form of Haworthia cymbiformis forms a low, stemless rosette of plump, boat-shaped leaves striped irregularly in light green and creamy white, with translucent leaf-tip windows still visible through the variegation. Because the pale, chlorophyll-poor stripes are more prone to sunburn or reversion in very low light, give it brighter placement than a typical haworthia while still protecting it from harsh direct midday sun. It offsets readily around the base to form a tight cluster that can be divided every couple of years, and sends up slender stalks to 8 inches tall bearing small, tubular, white-to-pale-pink flowers with brownish-green veins from mid-spring to early summer.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America
